- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast peak by 5–10% if followed by a spike.
- If sentiment is negative (≤ 0.33) and price is trending down, model often underestimates the drop; adjust downward by 3–8% to match true decline.
- After a sharp price spike (forecast > 75), model frequently overcorrects and overshoots in next 3–5 days; cap forecast at +5% above peak or use mean-reversion anchor.
- If sentiment is mixed or neutral (0.33–0.67), model often fails to capture mean reversion; apply 1–3% downward bias in mid-term (10–20d) forecasts.
- When sentiment is consistently low (e.g., 0.33 or below for 3+ days), model tends to ignore downward momentum; apply 2–5% downward adjustment to 30d forecast.
- If model forecast is > 76 and true outcome is < 74, sentiment was likely negative or neutral — reduce forecast by 5–10% to avoid overconfidence bias.
- For 30d forecasts, if last 3–5 days of sentiment are positive but price is falling, model often misreads trend — apply 2–5% downward correction to avoid “sentiment trap.”
